correctness.rationale: The revised finding gives exact identification width relative to the prime-order family in the same named-zero ternary relation. For any distinct names a,b the recursive D_n(a,b) has spare name c, and the only possible rebinding of b in D_n(a,c) is internal to that conjunct. It does not bind b in the adjacent addition atom, nor does any recursion bind the anchor a. Inductively the witness has value na and the atom requires b to be that witness plus a. With n=r−1 the closing atom asserts nonzero r-torsion, which in order p holds iff p=r, including r=2 via D_1. For the lower bound all ternary atoms on 0,x,y reduce to equality, doubling, negation or two-torsion tests: an occurrence of 0 in a sum slot is equality, 0 as output tests inverse or two-torsion, and the remaining cases are doubling or cancellation. Thus with a nonzero old anchor at prime order ≥7 only the choices 0,x,2x,x/2,−x and the complement matter. The five choices are distinct and the complement is nonempty at every such prime; this gives a permanent two-pebble response in either direction, with stationary zero and empty starts handled by zero/nonzero. The small primes have the stated distinguishing sentences, and all odd primes agree on the available one-name atomic types. Ground atoms in 0 agree at every prime. The frozen four-class finding is correct but prior; the repaired RESULT.md proves the exact-width statement and credits that lower bound. The supplied checker and output report 91 comparisons among 14 primes and 49 three-variable evaluations; these are finite diagnostics, not the unrestricted proof, and the uploaded script was not executed.

value.rationale: The number of variable names is a natural resource in the standard relational representation of a group, where functional terms are unavailable. The repair improves the compared five-name separation bound in the unrestricted-depth regime and pins down the exact least width by matching the established two-name lower bound. It identifies how much pebbled state is needed to recover the characteristic for every prime, not a tiny computation or an arbitrary numerical restriction. The argument is elementary, but its width/depth tradeoff and sharpness are the substantive point.
